version: arXiv:1509.08344v1 [math.PR], 28 September 2015; 8 PDF pages. The source title page prints ‘Schatte Model’; identity has not been changed to ‘Schatten’.

read_ranges.scope: 逐行阅读全部8页：定理与定义、三个 blocking/variance 引理、定理完整证明、文内外引说明和参考文献。

topic_relevance.K04: direct (empirical-process/strong-approximation branch). The result is a Gaussian strong approximation for an empirical CDF built from the dependent sequence of fractional parts {xS_k} of an iid-increment random walk. It is highly specialized, is not iid empirical-process theory, and provides no Gaussian-max anti-concentration inequality.

definitions.name: random-walk fractional-part empirical process
definitions.statement: X_i are iid real increments, S_k=X_1+…+X_k, x is a fixed nonzero scalar, and F_n(s)=n^(−1)Σ_{k≤n}1{{xS_k}≤s}, s∈[0,1]. The centered periodic indicator is f_s(u)=1{u≤s}−s on a unit period, extended periodically. The observations {xS_k} are dependent although the increments X_i are iid.

definitions.name: long-run covariance kernel
definitions.statement: For U∼Unif(0,1) independent of the increments, Γ(s,t)=s(1−t)+Σ_{r≥1}E[f_s(U)f_t(U+xS_r)]+Σ_{r≥1}E[f_t(U)f_s(U+xS_r)]. The paper's proof obtains exponential decay of the lag covariance under its bounded-density assumption. This covariance includes both lag directions and generally is not identified with the Brownian-bridge covariance without additional conditions.

definitions.name: shifted block-independence lemma (external to this paper's proof)
definitions.statement: Lemma 1 assumes a bounded, mean-zero, 1-periodic measurable f with L2 translation modulus ||f(·+h)−f||_{L2[0,1]}≤C h^(1/2). For separated index blocks with gaps ℓ, it asserts the existence of small random shifts δ_j, |δ_j|≤Ce^(−λℓ), not depending on f, such that the block sums Σ_{i∈I_1}f(S_i), Σ_{i∈I_2}f(S_i−δ_1), … are independent. The article says this first lemma was proved in an earlier manuscript and supplies no proof here.

theorem_cards.label: Main theorem (Gaussian strong approximation for the dependent empirical CDF)
assumptions: X_1,X_2,… are iid; X_1 is bounded and has a bounded density.
x≠0 is fixed (the proof states it is enough to prove x=1). No uniformity in x is claimed.
The probability space may be enlarged to construct the Gaussian approximants.
theorem_cards.statement: Let F_n(s)=n^(−1)Σ_{k≤n}1{{xS_k}≤s}. There are mean-zero Gaussian processes K_n(s) on [0,1] with covariance Γ_n(s,t) such that, for every exponent a<1/8, sup_{s,t∈[0,1]}|Γ_n(s,t)−Γ(s,t)|=O(n^(−a)); and for every γ<1/16, sup_{s∈[0,1]}|√n(F_n(s)−s)−K_n(s)|=O(n^(−γ)) almost surely. K_n is n-dependent through its covariance Γ_n; the result does not state a coupling to one fixed limiting Gaussian process.
proof_steps: By a scaling reduction the proof treats x=1. Partition the walk indices into long blocks I_k of order n^a and short blocks J_k of order n^b, with about n^(1−a) block pairs. Apply Lemma 1 to create shifts Δ_k and Π_k that make the long-block and short-block sums separately independent; show the shift error in the indicator sums is small.

Lemma 2 computes the long-block variance as asymptotic to nA(f), and the short-block variance as asymptotic to n^(1−b)A(f), where A(f)=||f||_2²+2Σ_{r≥1}E[f(U)f(U+S_rx)]. Lemma 3 gives the increment control A(f_{t−s})≤B(t−s)log((t−s)^(−1)).

Discretize s on a mesh n^(−ε), form vectors of centered block indicators on all mesh points, and apply the quoted Berthet–Mason independent-vector Gaussian coupling separately to the long and short block sequences. Under 1/2−γ>5ε/2+a, a>b, and a−b>2γ, Borel–Cantelli controls the grid error and removes the rescaled short-block Gaussian term.

Bernstein's inequality with Lemmas 2–3 controls fluctuations between adjacent mesh points. A mesh covariance estimate plus the modulus bound gives sup|Γ_n−Γ|≤C(log n)n^(−ε), and ε>a transfers this to the stated polynomial covariance rates.

The proof optimizes the block and mesh exponents and claims every γ<1/16. The final optimization paragraph contains a printed sign mismatch: it writes 1/2−γ>5ε/2−a, but the earlier condition (6) has +a and the next algebraic line γ<1/2−a−5ε/2 uses +a. The stated 1/16 optimization follows from the earlier +a condition, not from the printed minus-sign condition as written.
gaps: Lemma 1 is stated but not proved here; the authors refer to a previous manuscript. Its simultaneous-in-f property is central to the independent-block construction.
The finite-dimensional strong coupling is imported from Berthet–Mason [1], Lemma 4; the cited lemma is not reproduced or independently verified in this source review.

The last optimization paragraph has the explicit sign inconsistency recorded above. The proof's earlier displayed parameter condition and later algebra support +a; a literal reading of the later −a condition does not yield its next claimed inequality.

The assumptions are specialized to bounded iid increments with bounded density and a fixed nonzero frequency x. There is no claim for arbitrary dependent observations, unbounded increments, singular increment laws, or x→0 uniformly.

This is a strong-approximation result for one empirical-CDF index s and a dependent random-walk orbit; it is not a reusable anti-concentration theorem or a generic whole-class empirical-process result.

theorem_cards.label: Lemmas 2–3 (long-run variance and increment modulus)
assumptions: The block construction and shift bounds of Lemma 1 are in force; f is a centered periodic indicator or an increment f_{t−s} in the indicated periodic class.
The uniform phase U is independent of the increments; the bounded-density assumption supplies exponential lag covariance decay.
theorem_cards.statement: Lemma 2 states Σ_{k≤ℓ}Var(T_k(f_t))∼A(f_t)n and Σ_{k≤ℓ}Var(T_k^*(f_t))∼A(f_t)n^(1−b). Lemma 3 states A(f_{t−s})≤B(t−s)log((t−s)^(−1)) for a suitable B. These supply the local variance scale used in Bernstein interpolation and covariance control.
proof_steps: For Lemma 2, expand block variance into diagonal and lagged covariance sums. Replace shifted expectations by unshifted ones using exponentially small shift bounds; replace the distribution of S_j mod 1 by a uniform phase with exponentially small error; sum the lag covariance series into A(f). The short-block calculation is stated to be analogous.
For Lemma 3, write A(f_h)=h−h²+2Σ_{r≥1}E[f_h(U)f_h(U+S_rx)], bound each covariance by min(h,Ce^(−λr)), split the series at r≈log(1/h), and obtain O(h log(1/h)).
gaps: The proofs invoke the unproved shift-coupling Lemma 1 and exponential lag-decay facts under the density condition.
At zero-variance endpoints f_0 and f_1 are identically zero; the asymptotic-equivalence notation in Lemma 2 is not separately discussed for those degenerate indices.

constant_dependence: The theorem uses O(·) constants without a full dependence ledger. They may depend on the increment distribution, its bounded support and density bound, fixed frequency x, and the periodic-function/modulus constants. The covariance kernel depends on the full lag law through the summable series. The proof rate exponents arise from the block sizes, mesh exponent and the Berthet–Mason coupling; the source's parameter-optimization sign inconsistency prevents treating the final 1/16 calculation as fully self-consistent without resolving the typo in favor of the earlier condition.
endpoint_limits: The theorem excludes x=0 and gives no uniformity over nonzero x.
The increment law must be bounded and have a bounded density; these conditions are used for exponential mixing/lag decay and are not optional in the proof as written.
The approximating Gaussian process K_n is indexed by n and has covariance Γ_n; Γ_n→Γ does not itself identify all K_n on one common limiting-process coupling.
The stated rates are strict exponents a<1/8 and γ<1/16, not endpoint O(n^(−1/8)) or O(n^(−1/16)) claims.
The final printed optimization condition has −a where equation (6) and the subsequent derivation need +a; preserve this source-level ambiguity in any reuse of the optimal exponent.
reusable_methods: For a dependent empirical CDF indexed by thresholds, a periodic centered indicator can satisfy the L2 translation modulus needed by separated-block coupling; shift blocks to exact independence while quantifying the L2 shift error.

A covariance kernel for a stationary/mod-1 orbit naturally consists of the one-time Brownian-bridge term plus both directed lag covariance series; use the long-run variance functional A(f) to control increments.

A finite threshold mesh plus a Gaussian vector coupling, variance-based Bernstein interpolation, and a separate covariance-modulus calculation can turn finite-dimensional couplings into uniform-in-threshold strong approximation, provided every block and mesh exponent condition is checked.
unchecked: The previous-manuscript proof of Lemma 1 and Berthet–Mason [1], Lemma 4 were not independently read or verified.
No external numerical calculation or simulation was run; visual checks were used for formulas and the printed optimization sign.
The proof argument has not been independently reconstructed from first principles; this card records source claims, inspected derivation structure, and its explicit internal sign mismatch.
